name: North Carolina
overview: North Carolina counties do not sell tax lien certificates; they collect delinquent property taxes by foreclosing on the land and selling the property itself. A county can foreclose either through a court action in the nature of a mortgage foreclosure, where the judgment appoints a commissioner who sells the property by public auction to the highest bidder, or through the in rem method, where the tax collector files a certificate with the clerk of superior court and the sheriff sells the property like other real property sold under execution. After the auction the high bid stays open for upset bids: anyone may raise it by at least five percent, with a minimum increase of $750, and each upset bid starts a new 10-day period. Once the sale is confirmed the commissioner delivers the deed on payment of the price, and the buyer takes the property free and clear of most claims; the owner can stop the foreclosure by paying before the sale is confirmed, but there is no redemption period after it.

overview_sources.quote: The foreclosure action authorized by this section is in the nature of an action to foreclose a mortgage
The judgment shall appoint a commissioner to conduct the sale and shall order that the property be sold in fee simple.
The sale shall be by public auction to the highest bidder.
In case of redemption before confirmation of the foreclosure sale,
The judgment of confirmation shall direct the commissioner to deliver the deed upon payment of the purchase price.
the real property shall be sold by the sheriff in the same manner as other real property is sold under execution
The purchaser at the execution sale acquires title to the property in fee simple free and clear of all claims, rights, interests, and liens.
by a minimum of five percent (5%) thereof,
but in any event with a minimum increase of seven hundred fifty dollars ($750.00).
there may be successive upset bids, each of which shall be followed by a period of 10 days for a further upset bid.

counties.office: Wake County Department of Tax Administration (sales executed by the Wake County Sheriff's Office)
counties.next_sale_note: No sale dated yet: the foreclosure list (updated October 22, 2026) shows 'Date of Sale: To Be Announced' for each property. The county updates dates as the Sheriff's Office provides them.
counties.how_to_bid: Sales are public auctions run by the Sheriff's Office at the Wake County Courthouse (Salisbury Street entrance); notice is published 20 days before the auction. The successful bidder must make a cash deposit of 10% of the bid. The bid then stays open 10 days for upset bids of at least 5% of the current bid or $750, whichever is greater, filed with the Clerk of Superior Court on the 1st floor of the courthouse. Properties are sold as-is.

counties.next_sale_note: Sale dates are set as needed.
counties.how_to_bid: Attend the auction in person; only bids from auction attendees are accepted. The high bidder pays a deposit of 5% - 20% of the bid (per the Notice of Sale) in cash, money order or certified funds. Upset bids of at least 5% over the last bid (minimum increase $750) are filed in person at the Civil Department, 1st floor, Forsyth County Courthouse, with the court case number, during the 10-day upset period. Final payment is due at the foreclosure attorney's office on delivery of the Commissioner's Deed, no later than 30 days after the upset period ends. Properties are sold as is.

counties.how_to_bid: Attend the sale in the lobby of the Durham County Judicial Building. The high bidder pays a deposit of 10% of the bid on sale day (a personal check must be replaced with cash or certified funds within two hours). Upset bids of 5% or $750.00, whichever is greater, are filed with the Clerk of Court, and each starts a new 10-day period. The final high bidder must pay the balance within three business days or lose the deposit. Properties are sold as-is.
